prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level and opened laboratory tests of gravitational redshift, constants and dark matter

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as the sole prize part, and the second round has strengthened my reasons rather than only my comfort with the credit. The Secretary's test is whether the discovery is truly groundbreaking before anyone asks who deserves it. My answer, in one sentence, to the chair's question on the 2005 and 2012 prizes: the comb gave us a ruler for optical frequencies and ion control gave us single quantum systems as clocks, whereas the lattice clock showed that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a lattice at the magic wavelength with the trapping light cancelled out of the clock transition, so that statistical power and accuracy improve together and the result is reproduced at 10^-18 in several independent laboratories. That is a new regime of nature that can be probed, not a refinement of an existing apparatus. The proof is what has been measured with it: gravitational redshift across a millimetre, limits on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and many-body effects inside the clock itself. These are clues from nature obtained by measurement, which is the evidence I trust over elegant theory that has not been confirmed. The citation should rest on this demonstrated physics and not on the pending redefinition of the second, which I would treat as a consequence and leave out of the motivation. The credit is the pair that every member who proposed laureates for B002 named, Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for the accuracy and stability records and the many-body clock work. I do not think a second distinct achievement is needed. The statutes allow one achievement, and adding a part would only force us to accept a weaker candidate to fill a number.
statement.case_against: The objection that survives round 1 is the one the chair framed, discovery versus technique. A sceptical reader will say that clocks are an instrument whose lineage has been honoured already (Ramsey, Hall and Hansch, Wineland and Haroche) and that Ye shared the 2005 prize. I think the sentence above answers it, but a sentence in a citation is not the same as persuading the wider community, and I accept that Mehlig and Pearce read this differently. A second worry is that I am the member who has moved the furthest, from the Higgs experiments first in my opening to clocks first now, and six members in the files have converged on B002 largely after reading one another. I should not mistake that convergence for independent confirmation. If the committee is comfortable with a leadership-based credit, the Higgs discovery is the larger event in physics and my preference would go back to it. Finally the priority question is still open: the magic-wavelength idea, the first strontium lattice clock and the later accuracy record may not sit as cleanly with Katori and Ye as our shorthand suggests, and I am working from memory rather than the original papers.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality as a compact, mature, conceptually central result with an independently reproduced experimental confirmation, and he asks whether lattice clocks are a discovery or a technology.
responses.response: I take his discovery-versus-technology question seriously, and I admire the conceptual reach of KPZ, since universality across growth, polymers and random matrices is the sort of idea that I would expect to last. But the test I apply is whether nature has been probed and confirmed in a way that the committee can write in a citation. Here his own concession decides it for me: Parisi and the exact-solution authors are outside the three names, and the experimental confirmation rests mostly on one liquid-crystal system, as Kroll and Lindroth noted. The prize would honour the 1986 equation and one experiment, not the full structure he finds compelling. Lattice clocks, by contrast, make a new quantity measurable that was not before, and that is a clue from nature obtained across laboratories. I do not think the objection to clocks is empty, but I think it is answered by the redshift, constants and dark-matter results.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether credit for the first demonstration belongs to Katori and the accuracy records to Ye, wants the priority of the magic-wavelength idea checked against the record, and has weakened her own preference for magic-angle graphene.
responses.response: Her question is the right one to put to Lindroth and Kroll, and I would ask them to report on the early-2000s chronology before the ballot. My understanding is that Katori's group made the lattice proposal and the first strontium demonstration, and that Ye's group then drove the accuracy and stability, and the redshift and many-body results. I do not regard that as two separate prizes, because the discovery here is the lattice regime and not only its first sighting, and both halves were needed before the community believed it. If the record shows that a parallel proposal predates Katori's, I would change the wording of the citation, not the pair, since no member has proposed another. I also welcome her move away from twisted bilayer graphene, and I agree that the pairing mechanism and Cao's absence make it too early.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the citation state explicitly what is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and asks whether a three-person prize could be completed with a second achievement without weakening the clean B002 pair.
responses.response: I agree on the first point and have tried to write the distinction into the citation, naming magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and not clocks in general. On the second, I do not see a second part that improves the prize. Each candidate that could be added brings an open problem of its own: a collaboration-credit question for B053, the DUMAND and Baikal lineage for B043, the 2016 overlap and unsettled credit for B015, and the unsettled mechanism for B038. A clean two-person B002 is a better outcome than a two-part prize with a contested half. I would only change this if she or Kroll found that the Sr and Yb community needs a third name, and my reading of the statements is that nobody wants that.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new state of matter confirmed by experiment, and raises whether the emphasis should be a state of matter or a precision-measurement capability.
responses.response: I accept his framing that the discovery should be about nature, and that is exactly why I read clocks as more than an instrument. But I still cannot support the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio for the reasons he himself gives. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, Zhang has died, the 3D contributors are outside the names, and the 2016 prize on topological phases will make many readers ask what is new. A citation that omits the HgTe prediction would be unfair, and one that includes it breaks the three-name limit. I would be glad to see it honoured under another configuration, but not at the cost of a defensible credit.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, moved B002 ahead of IceCube, but says that if the committee wants a first-of-its-kind discovery about nature then B043 is the stronger statement and B053 is more consequential if a rule-compliant credit exists.
responses.response: I share his reading of B043 and B053 and I have kept them as my alternatives for those reasons. On B053 I cannot offer the statutory argument the chair asks for: spokespersons and project leaders are not by that fact the people who made the 2012 measurement, and I would not want to defend such a credit line by line. On B043 I regard the diffuse flux as secure, but the source picture is thin and the pioneers from DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA are a real credit problem, so I would not put it ahead of a precision result that is already reproduced. I do not move on this because of his support count, but because his own caveats on the other two lead to the same place.

uncertainties: Whether the early priority of the magic-wavelength lattice and the first strontium lattice clock sits with Katori in the way our shorthand suggests, which I have not checked against the original papers.
Whether the wider community will accept the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a difference in discovery and not only in technique.
Whether the convergence on B002 in the round-1 files, reached partly after members read one another's openings, reflects independent judgement or shared anchoring.
Whether a rule-compliant credit for the Higgs experiments exists, which would make B053 the larger prize and is the position I could still move back to.
My assessment of ATLAS, CMS and IceCube leadership roles comes from background knowledge and has not been verified against the committee record.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile shows no specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate. Gross, Rubinstein and Van Riet, my mentors and co-author, work in string theory and have no connection to any shortlisted ballot. As Secretary I commission outside reports, but that is a procedural role and not a personal tie to any candidate. I have no connection to Katori or Ye.
